messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Public Transport: Bus riding, Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Vignette:
Aisha was 25, a South Asian American woman who worked as a counselor and had been living on her own, unmarried, and trying to keep her life looking steady from the outside. The event she now described as the turning point happened after an encounter with police in her neighborhood, when what had begun as a tense public situation escalated into violence and left her feeling physically overpowered and humiliated. In the weeks that followed, she found that the memory did not stay in one form. At times she could speak about it in a flat, disconnected way, as if she were describing something that had happened to someone else entirely, her voice going quiet and her face unreadable. At other times, it came back with startling force: she would suddenly feel again the same bodily position she had been in during the incident, and the scene would seem to arrive all at once through her senses, as if she were back inside it rather than remembering it from a distance. She said there were moments when the smell of soil or damp outdoor air would catch her off guard and bring the whole thing rushing back so completely that she could almost feel the same air on her skin, even when she was standing far from where it happened.

Since then, Aisha had organized much of her life around trying not to be caught unprepared. She noticed that her body seemed to react before she had fully taken in what was happening, so even ordinary moments could put her on edge. When she was outside, she watched people’s faces and body language closely, studying who looked tense, who held themselves like an officer, who might be about to confront her. The sight of police presence was especially potent; she described a sudden tightening in her chest and a readiness to move away before she had time to tell herself she was safe. Riding the bus had become another difficult part of daily life. She used public transport for work and errands, but on crowded buses she felt trapped in a way that reminded her of the original event, especially if a uniformed officer boarded or if a sudden stop made everyone shift at once. She would sit rigidly near the door when she could, scanning the faces around her, aware that she was no longer just commuting but bracing herself.

At work, these changes had become difficult to hide. As a counselor, Aisha was expected to sit calmly with other people’s distress, yet she found herself distracted by the simple fact of being in close proximity to strangers, especially if any part of their posture or tone seemed authoritative or unpredictable. She began avoiding social contact with people she had known and spent time with before the incident. Friends from her community, people she had once seen regularly, now felt complicated to her; seeing them made her aware of how much had changed, and she did not want to have to answer questions or appear not to be herself. She said that what frightened her most was the sense that people were not what they seemed. Before the incident, she had assumed she could read a situation by appearance or tone, but now she doubted that assumption and kept herself guarded even in familiar places.

Aisha also struggled with the feeling that the event had left something in her permanently altered. She used words like dirty and contaminated to describe how she felt in relation to what happened, even though she could not point to anything visible that had been done to her. There was a painful sense that she had lost her connection to her community and culture, not because she had chosen to step away, but because she no longer felt able to move through those spaces with ease. Family gatherings, neighborhood events, and even casual contact with other South Asian families felt distant to her, as though the person who once belonged there had been separated from that life. She often covered her face with her hands when she felt exposed or overwhelmed, and at home she found herself checking mirrors repeatedly, as if needing to confirm who and where she was after the memory or the day’s tension had unsettled her. Falling asleep was difficult because she felt she had to stay alert, and nighttime did not bring relief so much as another period in which she needed to remain watchful.

By the time she sought help, Aisha was worn down by the effort of managing these experiences alone. She had begun to miss the ease she once had in ordinary routines, including riding the bus without calculating every seat and every face. What finally brought her to treatment was the realization that she no longer felt fully present in her own life, and that her work, her relationships, and her sense of belonging had all become narrower than they used to be. She came hoping to feel less trapped by the memory and less alarmed by the world around her, but she was also afraid that the event had changed her in a way she could not undo.
